description: Multi-dimensional adversarial review of a diff or capability: correctness, security, and spec compliance, with every finding adversarially verified before it is reported.

findings.title: Task Publish/Unpublish is enabled while the task form has unsaved edits, so the stored version is published
findings.evidence: `<Button disabled={busy} onClick={() => void changeStatus()}>` is the only guard. `setTaskStatus(task.taskId, next)` publishes the server copy, so edits still in TaskEditor's local `form` state (prompt, answer key) are left out without warning. The mission editor in the same slice blocks exactly this case with `disabled={busy || dirty}` and the `admin.missionEditor.saveFirst` hint (MissionEditorScreen.tsx:332-335). The two publish flows behave differently, and an admin can publish a task they think includes their fix.
findings.suggestion: Pass a `dirty` flag from TaskEditor, comparing `form` with `initialForm(task, …)` or a saved snapshot, into TaskStatusPanel. Disable publish while it is true and show a 'save first' hint, the same way MissionEditor does. Also share `busy` so publishing can't race an in-flight save.

findings.title: A stale save-error alert stays on screen after a later publish or delete succeeds
findings.evidence: `changeStatus` and `destroy` clear `saveStatus`, `actionStatus` and `actionError`, but not `saveError` or `errors`. A save can fail on an unchanged mission (for example a 409 position clash or a network error), and in that case `dirty` is false so Publish stays enabled. If Publish then succeeds, the screen shows the old `ConflictAlert` from the save (role=alert) next to the 'published' status, which contradicts it.
findings.suggestion: Call `setSaveError(null)` (and clear `errors` if appropriate) at the start of `changeStatus` and `destroy`, just as `save` clears the action state.

findings.title: Every 409 from a task save is described as a mission conflict
findings.evidence: `if (error instanceof ApiError && error.status === 409) setConflict(error);` routes every 409 to `<ConflictAlert error={conflict} describe={describeMission} />`. Some 409s may not be mission-related (for example source/page locks or `conflicts` ids that are task or source ids). Their ids then show as 'unknown item' ids, with no link. A 409 that also has field-path errors gets both the field errors and the alert.
findings.suggestion: Only use describeMission when the conflict ids resolve to missions, or let the describe callback fall back to the task or source. Keep the field-error branch first, so a 409 that has a field path lands only on its field.

findings.title: Publish/unpublish and delete on the mission and source screens don't share a busy guard
findings.evidence: `destroy(mission)` doesn't set `busy`, and DeleteControl keeps its own separate `busy`. So Publish (or Save) and Delete can both be in flight together. If the delete succeeds after a publish has started, the publish's `refresh(result)` puts the deleted mission back into the cache with `setQueryData(missionKey(...))`. SourceEditForm has the same gap between `save` and `destroy`.
findings.suggestion: Set the screen-level `busy` around `destroy`, and pass `disabled={busy || …}` to DeleteControl. Or disable the other actions while a delete confirmation is pending.

findings.title: The source grade select can show a value different from the one it submits
findings.evidence: `meta.grade` is set from `String(source.grade)`, but the options come only from `reference.grades`. If the stored grade is no longer in the reference list, the browser displays the first option while state keeps the old grade. Saving then sends a grade the admin never saw.
findings.suggestion: If `meta.grade` isn't in `reference.grades`, add an option for it (for example marked as unavailable), so the controlled value always matches a visible option.

result.reasoning: The finding holds. `TaskStatusPanel.tsx:60` disables the button only on its own `busy`. `TaskEditorScreen.tsx:427` renders `<TaskStatusPanel task={task} onDeleted={onDeleted} />` and passes no dirty or busy state, even though the editor keeps the edits in local `form` state (line 77) that is only sent by `save()`. `changeStatus()` calls `setTaskStatus(task.taskId, next)`, which changes the status of the stored copy and never sends `form`. So an admin can edit the prompt or answer key, click Publish without saving, and publish the old version with no warning. Nothing else guards this path: there is no dirty check in the task editor, no confirm dialog, and the panel's `busy` is separate from the editor's `busy`, so a publish can also run during an in-flight save. The two publish flows in the same slice really do behave differently. Rating it major is reasonable because no data is lost (the unsaved edits stay in the form and can still be saved), but the admin can be misled about what gets published.

The finding holds; I couldn't refute it. `TaskStatusPanel` is rendered on the same screen as the editable form, below it (`TaskEditorScreen.tsx:427`), whenever a saved task is loaded. How to reproduce:
1. Open `/admin/tasks/edit?taskId=X` for a draft task.
2. Change the prompt or the answer key, and don't press Save.
3. Press Publish.

The old stored version is published and the panel shows a "published" status. The unsaved edits stay in the form, so the admin can easily believe the fix went live.

The finding holds for publish and unpublish. It does not hold for delete.

**What the code does**
- `changeStatus` (lines 135–150) clears `saveStatus`, `actionStatus` and `actionError`. It never clears `saveError` or `errors`.
- Line 269 shows a save failure through `FormAlert`, and line 270 shows it through `ConflictAlert`. Both stay on screen until something resets that state.

2. `isDirty(form, saved)` is still false, so the Publish/Unpublish button at line 328 stays enabled.

- **Example:** a position clash probably comes back as a field error (`fieldErrors`). That would show in `errors`/`FormAlert`, not in `ConflictAlert`. A network error is a cleaner example.

The core mechanism is confirmed: the stale save error survives a successful status change. Keeping severity at minor, since it is a cosmetic or messaging issue with no data impact.

The finding holds: the missing guard is real and a user can reach it. The harm it describes, though, is narrow and not visible to the user, so the severity should go down.

**The missing guard is real.** In `MissionEditorScreen.tsx`:
- `destroy` (lines 152-165) never calls `setBusy`.
- `DeleteControl` (lines 340-345) only gets `disabled={!saved.deletable}`. Its own `busy` state (`DeleteControl.tsx` lines 24 and 39-44) only disables its own Delete and Cancel buttons.
- So after clicking Publish/Unpublish (or Save), the user can open the delete question and confirm it while the first request is still running. The reverse also works: while a delete is running, Publish is still enabled (`disabled={busy || dirty}`) because `busy` was never set.

**Nothing on the server blocks it.** The contract defines `AdminMission.deletable` by attempts, reports and opened hints only (`openapi.yaml:1758`). A published mission can still be deleted, so both requests can succeed.

**The cache write does happen.** `refresh()` calls `setQueryData(missionKey(id), result)` (line 100). If the publish response is handled after `destroy` has run `removeQueries` (line 158), the deleted mission is written back into the cache.

**Why the impact is small:**
1. **The ordering is unlikely.** The publish must commit on the server before the delete (otherwise it gets a 404 and never calls `refresh`), yet its response must reach the client after the delete's response. That mostly needs lock contention or reordered responses, plus a two-click confirmation fired inside one request's round trip.
2. **The stale entry can't really be seen:**
   - Once `deleted` is true, the component only shows the "deleted" view (line 167), whatever is in the cache.
   - `MISSIONS_KEY` (`['admin','missions']`) is invalidated, so the list drops the row.
   - `missionKey` is `['admin','mission',id]` and uses the default `staleTime` of 0 (`queryClient.ts` has no override). Opening that URL again therefore refetches, gets a 404, and `MissionEditorScreen` checks for the 404 error first and shows "not found". At worst the old editor flashes until that refetch finishes.
   - Nothing is corrupted on the server, and no wrong action can follow from the stale entry.

**Save + Delete** has the same shape and the same small impact: if the delete wins, the save gets a 404 and its error is hidden behind the deleted view. If the save wins, the same stale entry appears as above.

**Verdict:** a real gap in the UI's concurrency handling, but the consequence is a short-lived cache entry with nearly no user impact. It should be a nit or hardening item rather than a correctness bug. The suggested fix (share `busy` and pass `disabled={busy || !saved.deletable}`) is still cheap and worth doing.

The React behaviour described is real: a controlled `<select>` whose value matches no `<option>` shows the first option. But I couldn't find a way for a real user to hit it, and even if one did, it does no harm.

1. **No type mismatch.** `ReferenceData.grades` is `number[]` (schema.d.ts:887). The options render `value={g}`, which becomes the string "6". `meta.grade` is `String(source.grade)`, also "6". So any stored grade that is in the list matches its option.
2. **A stored grade can't be missing from the list in normal use.** The schema says `SourceMetadata.grade` / `SourceUpdate.grade` must be "One of ReferenceData.grades" (schema.d.ts:903 and 913), and the server enforces it when a source is created. The MVP configures only `[6]`. A stale grade would need an operator to remove a grade from server config while sources still use it. Nothing in the frontend, the contract or the MVP plan does that. It's hypothetical config drift, not a user or attacker path.
3. **Even then, nothing bad is sent.** The form would submit the source's existing, unchanged grade. That's not "a grade the admin never saw" in any harmful sense, because it's exactly what is stored. The backend either accepts it as unchanged (a locked grade only refuses changes, per CA-D16) or rejects it as not configured. A rejection comes back through `fieldErrors` and shows on the grade field. Nothing is silently corrupted.
4. The subject select has the same theoretical pattern. That supports the view that this is a general UI-hardening idea, not a reachable bug.

The finding is low confidence and I couldn't confirm a reproducible path, so I'm marking it refuted. At most it's a nit about future config drift.

But calling them NFR-9 violations misreads how the project has defined and enforces NFR-9. 1. The finding guesses that the pseudo-catalog test "probably ignores bare punctuation and digits" by accident. It does not. The exemption is deliberate and written down. `src/app/i18n-coverage.test.tsx:17-24` defines `COVERED` and `NO_WORDS` (`/^[\s\d\p{P}\p{S}]*$/u`) with the comment "Separators and numbers carry no words; the lint rule allows them too." 2. The NFR-9 lint rule says the same thing. `eslint-rules/no-literal-ui-text.js:19` reads: "Allows punctuation-only text (" · ", "/"), whitespace, and every expression." The parts that carry words are already handled: `topicName` is marked `data-content`, and the position text comes from `t('admin.missions.label')`. So nothing is broken here.
